lesson.title: The Zero That Isn't Quite Zero
lesson.summary: Real op-amps need a tiny differential voltage between their inputs to make the output sit at zero, and that mismatch gets multiplied by the circuit's gain into a real DC error at the output.
lesson.body:
In the ideal op-amp model, tying the inverting and non-inverting inputs to the same voltage forces the output to zero (relative to whatever reference the circuit uses). Real op-amps cannot quite manage that. The differential pair of transistors inside the input stage is never perfectly matched: tiny manufacturing differences in the two transistors mean the amplifier actually needs a small, nonzero voltage difference between its inputs before its output settles at zero. That required voltage, referred back to the input, is called the input offset voltage, Vos. Datasheets list typical and maximum values, ranging from a few microvolts on precision parts to several millivolts on ordinary general-purpose parts.

Vos matters because a real circuit cannot tell the difference between "a real signal at the input" and "the offset voltage acting like a tiny signal at the input." Both get amplified by whatever gain the feedback network sets, called the noise gain of the circuit. So even with the intended input signal at exactly zero, the output carries an error term equal to Vos times the noise gain.

Take the same non-inverting amplifier used for the bandwidth example: Rf = 99 kΩ, Rg = 1 kΩ, giving a gain of 1 + 99k/1k = 100. Suppose this particular op-amp has a typical Vos of 2 mV. Even with the input grounded, the output offset error is Vos x gain = 2 mV x 100 = 200 mV, or 0.2 V. That is not a small number: if this amplifier were meant to boost a millivolt-level sensor signal by 100x and report values near zero for a zero input, a 200 mV DC offset would swamp anything the sensor was actually trying to report.

Two practical fixes follow directly from the mechanism. First, choose an op-amp with lower Vos when the application needs precision at DC, precision instrumentation parts specify Vos in the tens of microvolts. Second, if only the AC content of a signal matters (audio, for instance), AC-couple the signal with a series capacitor or add a high-pass filter stage, which removes the DC offset along with any other DC component before it ever reaches later stages. Some op-amps also expose offset-null trim pins that let a small external potentiometer cancel the offset by hand, though this only corrects for the offset at one temperature and drifts as the part warms up.
